extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of rhetoric and oratory (classical/academic audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative and prescriptive principles from Aristotle's Rhetoric (Book 1, chapter 1) about what counts as good persuasive speech and how rhetoric differs from and relates to dialectic. Includes rules about proofs, enthymeme, audience/emotion management, legal/contextual constraints, and ethical cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric as counterpart to dialectic
rubrics_metrics.description: ῥητορική ἐστιν ἀντίστροφος τῇ διαλεκτικῇ — rhetoric is the counterpart/opposite of dialectic; both concern common topics rather than a specialized science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle frames rhetoric as sharing subject-matter with dialectic (topics 'common to all') and being accessible by habit or art. This situates rhetoric as a practical, teachable method for handling common controversies rather than an exact scientific discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: treatment of common, not specialized, matters
rubrics_metrics.description: περὶ τοιούτων τινῶν εἰσιν ἃ κοινὰ τρόπον τινά ἁπάντων ἐστὶ γνωρίζειν καὶ οὐδεμιᾶς ἐπιστήμης ἀφωρισμένης — rhetoric deals with matters that are in common and generally knowable, not with a narrowly defined scientific subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating rhetoric, favor arguments and topics that address commonly shared beliefs and probable matters rather than technical, narrowly specialized proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic proofs (pisteis) are central
rubrics_metrics.description: αἱ γὰρ πίστεις ἔντεχνόν εἰσι μόνον, τὰ δ᾽ ἄλλα προσθῆκαι — the 'pisteis' (means of persuasion) are the artful components; other elements are accessory/external.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on constructing the internal, artful means of persuasion (argumentative proofs, character, emotional appeals) rather than relying solely on external trappings; distinguish between what is produced by rhetorical art and what is merely added on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthymeme as rhetorical demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: ἀπόδειξις ῥητορική ἐνθύμημα ... ἐνθύμημα συλλογισμός τις — rhetorical demonstration is the enthymeme; an enthymeme is a kind of syllogism or abbreviated logical inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rhetorical arguments as enthymemes: structured, probable syllogistic reasoning appropriate to audiences. Study from what types of premises and by what means enthymemes arise; they are the principal rhetorical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim: show the probable, not deliver scientific certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: οὐ τὸ πεῖσαι ἔργον αὐτῆς, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἰδεῖν τὰ ὑπάρχοντα πιθανά — the work of rhetoric is not to establish scientific certainty but to make the existing things appear probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical success is measured by making a position seem plausible to the audience, not by achieving demonstrative (scientific) proof. Emphasize probability, likelihood, and plausibility in claims and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage emotions aimed at the judge (pathos as targeted)
rubrics_metrics.description: διαβολὴ...ἔλεος...ὀργὴ...πάθη τῆς ψυχῆς οὐ περὶ τοῦ πράγματός ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸν δικαστήν — emotions like slander, pity, and anger are not about the fact but are directed toward the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that emotional appeals operate on the audience/judge rather than on objective facts. Use pathos to influence judgment appropriately, but be aware it changes perception of the judge rather than altering the underlying truth of the matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect legal/contextual limits in judicial oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: ὁ νόμος κωλύει λέγειν ἔξω τοῦ πράγματος — law (and courtroom rules) often forbids speaking beyond the matter at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judicial contexts, adhere to procedural and legal constraints: avoid extraneous argumentation outside the facts of the case; judges and laws limit what is legitimate to argue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave matters beyond judges' knowledge as little as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: δεῖ ὡς ἐλαχίστων ποιεῖν κύριον τὸν κριτήν ... ἀνάγκη ἐπὶ τοῖς κριταῖς καταλείπειν — where possible make the judge the least possible authority on matters that cannot be known by them; avoid depending on judges to know things the lawgiver could not foresee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on the judge's special knowledge of disputed facts (past/future) — keep arguments tethered to what judges can reasonably assess; minimize assumptions about the judge's information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be able to argue and respond to the opposite side
rubrics_metrics.description: τἀναντία δεῖ δύνασθαι πείθειν ... οὐχ ὅπως ἀμφότερα πράττωμεν — rhetoric and dialectic alone consider opposites; one must be able to make plausible the contrary position (not to advocate the bad, but to see how things could be mistaken).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train to present and refute the opposing case; rhetorical skill requires understanding how the opposite might be argued so you can counter it and discern the truth by testing alternate arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical restraint: rhetoric can harm if misused
rubrics_metrics.description: εἰ δ᾽ ὅτι μεγάλα βλάψειεν ἂν ὁ χρώμενος ἀδίκως ... τοῦτό γε κοινόν ἐστι ... πλὴν ἀρετῆς — if one uses rhetorical power unjustly one could greatly harm most goods (power, wealth, health, strategy); only virtue is immune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the moral dangers of rhetoric: persuasive skill used unjustly can bring serious harm. Ethical restraint and concern for virtue should guide rhetorical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to external parts (preface, narration, arrangement) to shape the judge
rubrics_metrics.description: τί δεῖ τὸ προοίμιον ἢ τὴν διήγησιν ἔχειν, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἕκαστον μορίων — those who define the external parts (what the preface or narration should be) aim to make the judge of a certain sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose and order external elements (prooimion/introduction, narrative, arrangement) deliberately to form the judge/audience's disposition; these are not proofs themselves but shape how proofs are received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric as teachable method using common topics
rubrics_metrics.description: διδασκαλίας γάρ ἐστιν ... ἀνάγκη διὰ τῶν κοινῶν ποιεῖσθαι τὰς πίστεις — rhetorical speech is a form of teaching inasmuch as it uses common topics and constructs persuasive beliefs, not by scientific demonstration but by common reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical instruction should train speakers in common topoi and methods for producing persuasive beliefs; teaching focuses on practical methods for persuading many rather than on technical scientific proofs.
